Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan on why sovereign AI makes Cold War-style verification necessary:

"From my very idealistic perspective, I'm surprised to see so much investment in sovereign AI."

"You could probably consolidate a lot of these efforts. But it seems like that's not the world we're in or the one we're headed towards. There are actually increased efforts to build AI in a sovereign way."

"So that takes having a shared language to communicate about what the framework for evaluations is, and where we're going to collectively align around the risks."

"There's a lot to learn from nuclear here. Reagan had this line, 'Trust but verify.' We're starting to see signs of trust in that Xi Jinping and Trump are going to be meeting... But there is no clear way to actually do the verification part of this."

"Having the shared language of evals will allow us to say things like, you have the right number of nuclear warheads. In that example, there were also flyovers, a mechanism by which a country could audit another country's nuclear stockpile."

"If there's concern about the societal or even existential risk of AI, it will necessitate us constructing this shared language of evaluations to do the verification process."

@RayanKrishnan @JenniferHli

Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan on how they score a model's ability to build its own successor:

"One benchmark we released recently is our Recursive Self-Improvement Index. It's a topic which a lot of the big labs have been talking about and starting to report on in their model cards."

"There isn't a shared language to talk about the RSI potential of models. So we created this as an apples-to-apples way to actually benchmark across the models."

"In an ideal world, what you want to do is take a frontier model and have it train the next version of itself and see where the delta comes from. But obviously that's very expensive and slow."

"What we're doing is forming a set of proxies for every part of the process it takes to build the next version of the model."

"There's work around pre-training, post-training, harness-level engineering, and then seeing in which mechanisms and behaviors the models are able to do very good research work and build something new, and where they're struggling."

A former colleague of mine just shared one of my old business cycle indicators.

I built it. It stayed at Pictet when I left.

Funny thing about rebuilding a process from scratch... it forces you to revisit your old work with a fresh pair of eyes.

I've done it many times now. Every time, there are improvements to be made.

So let me be blunt about this one: it's dead.

It’s a composite. Labor market conditions, the yield curve, the output gap, profit margins, consumer sentiment, wages... roughly fifteen inputs, ranked in percentile.

Many of those inputs have lost their meaning in a K-shaped economy. They were built to read a broad, synchronized cycle, where labor, credit and profits moved together. That economy doesn't exist anymore. So the signal degrades.

You can see it plainly in the chart: the last time this indicator hit the 90th percentile, it should have called a recession. In the old world it would have. This time it didn’t.

The changes I've been writing about for the past eighteen months have broken most of these old-school macro models. Or at the very least, made them far less important than they used to be.

This is exactly why the loud voices calling for recession these past 2-3 years have all been wrong. I took the other side.

I explained why they were wrong... initially in a GMI piece last year, then more completely in one titled The Compute Cycle, one of the last pieces I wrote before I left GMI.

Here's the bigger issue.

Everyone is building dashboards now. AI handed the world a new set of power tools, and almost overnight, anyone could ship a model.

However, AI made it possible for anyone to build tools. What it has not done is make everyone a toolmaker.

The difference is judgment.

Most people have been handed the capability without the apprenticeship.

They can produce the model. They cannot tell you how it works. And if you can't do that, you can't refine it.

The oldest rule in this business does not care how good the technology gets: garbage in, garbage out.

This old chart of mine is not the only one.

The Financial Conditions Index I developed years ago… same story: dying.

Why?

Because the ground underneath these indicators is moving, and fast.

For forty years the business cycle lived inside a cage. That cage held through the dotcom bust, the Global Financial Crisis, COVID, and half a dozen Fed cycles.

Then this year global semiconductor sales posted the largest annual increase in over four decades, and the cage broke.

Compute stopped being a downstream input to the real-world production cycle and became the binding constraint.

Growth now starts with chips and propagates outward. Everything else sits downstream. And that guts the old financial conditions logic.

These frameworks were built for a world where cash flow sensitivity to rates, a strong dollar and high oil prices governed the cycle.

The dollar still matters, it always will, it's the price of global liquidity. Rates and oil still matter too. But their grip on the cycle has loosened.

When capex is funded off corporate balance sheets running a moonshot, and the buildout is a strategic imperative nobody can opt out of (the Red Queen Effect), those old transmission channels matter far less than they used to.

When the causality of the entire cycle flips, the tools built to read the old one don't just need tuning. They need burying.

For well over a decade I've built asset allocation models and business cycle frameworks for some of the most sophisticated investors in the world.

That work, and the discipline of staying relentlessly data-dependent, is what I'm known for.

The craft beneath it has always been the same. Statistics and econometrics. The unglamorous stuff you can't shortcut, and can't fake.

It comes with me on this next venture. A full suite of new indicators, built from the ground up.

I'll be sharing much more in Q4.

The macro landscape is shifting. More now than ever.

Time to sit up...
